title: Why Does Education Reform (Almost) Always Fail?
author: Robert VerBruggen
summary: Robert VerBruggen asks why education reforms that show promise in rigorous experiments tend to fizzle once they spread, drawing on a new paper by James Wyckoff on teacher evaluation. The Obama-era push led 44 states to adopt multi-tier evaluation systems, yet only a few districts such as Cincinnati, Dallas, Chicago, and Washington, DC saw meaningful achievement gains. Wyckoff argues that evaluation can work when implemented well, with gains of about a tenth of a standard deviation and better teachers staying while weaker ones leave. Most states left design to districts, and administrators were often poorly trained, pressed for time, and lenient, as shown by the Gates-funded Intensive Partnerships for Effective Teaching, where fewer than 1 percent of teachers were dismissed. VerBruggen generalises that half-hearted adoption, thin investment, resistance, and limited staff explain why good ideas rarely scale. He sees a modestly optimistic reading if failures can be diagnosed.
points: The pattern is that reforms succeed in tightly run pilots and weaken when adopted widely by staff who are less committed than the designers.
Teacher evaluation produced real if modest gains in some districts, so VerBruggen reads the failure as one of implementation rather than concept.
Leniency bias, poor training, and a lack of required rigor meant that very few teachers faced consequences even after the Gates investment.
The mechanism of differential retention assumes a supply of better teachers ready to replace those who leave.
He suggests diagnosing why reforms fail could improve later attempts, though nothing guarantees it.
quotes: Why does one reform after another show immense promise—and even produce big results in rigorous experiments—only to fizzle out when it gains wider implementation?

As Wyckoff summarizes, “Cincinnati, Dallas, Chicago, and Washington, DC produced meaningful achievement gains, while forty-four state systems, Houston, and a heavily funded, pre-screened seven-site demonstration produced little or none.
Administrators were often poorly trained, pressed for time, and overly lenient for fear of upsetting staff.
Because nearly all teachers received ratings of at least Effective, very few teachers were subject to dismissal or required improvement plans,” Wyckoff writes.
You might come up with a great idea to help kids learn better, and you might even pull off implementation in a few places, but it’s exceedingly difficult to spread a good idea widely in this area.

Most places will try the idea half-heartedly and give up when it doesn’t work. They won’t make the necessary investments, address new challenges as they arise, or overcome the inevitable resistance from defenders of the status quo.
In teacher evaluation, for example, the concept of differential retention assumes there are high-quality teachers waiting in reserve to join your district when you push the low-quality ones out.
